world.title: The Great ADHD Myth: What you need to know about Channel 4’s “most controversial show of the year” - The BMJ
world.summary: The documentary’s exploration of the rapid rise in diagnoses has made a splash, but many experts argue it presented a one sided view, as Jane Feinmann reports A Channel 4 television documentary screened this week—claimed by the Guardian to be the “most controversial show of the year”—has provoked a backlash from experts after airing claims that thousands of children are being drugged into socially acceptable behaviour by medications prescribed for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The Great ADHD Myth asked whether ADHD was a social construct or a treatable brain disease and concluded firmly that it was the first.1 After the programme was screened on Tuesday 18 August, one leading ADHD researcher who was interviewed said her comments were “cherry picked” and accused the documentary of being “biased.” The advocacy group ADHD UK filed a formal complaint with the communications watchdog Ofcom, arguing that the documentary “misled” viewers.2 And the Royal College of Psychiatrists (RCPsych) warned that questioning the validity of a well established neurodevelopmental condition harms patients and clinicians and misrepresents clinical consensus. The documentary was presented by Max Pemberton, a full time NHS psychiatrist who also writes a health advice column for the Daily Mail , in which he has often written about the rise in ADHD diagnoses.34 The vast majority of clinicians interviewed in the programme said they thought ADHD was a social construct rather than a genuine disorder.

clinical_trials.summary: A report reviewed by TrialSite News advances a provocative argument: optimizing vitamin D3, zinc and quercetin across the population could provide broader, safer and cheaper protection against RNA viruses than a vaccine-first strategy built around repeated mRNA vaccination.
